steps.say: Posterior urethral valves are the commonest severe plumbing blockage a baby boy can be born with, and they threaten both kidneys from the first weeks of life. Extra flaps of mucosa in the back urethra act as one way valves, letting urine out poorly while pressure builds upstream. They strike one in 4000 to 8000 live male births, so every urologist meets them early in training.
steps.tx: Recognise **posterior urethral valves** (**PUV**, back urethra flaps) as the commonest cause of congenital severe lower urinary tract obstruction in male neonates (**congenital obstruction**, born blocked), seen in **1 in 4000 to 8000** (one in four to eight thousand) live births. Mucosal folds valve the stream while pressure climbs to the kidneys, so PUV tops the differential of any newborn boy with a weak stream and palpable bladder.

vis.alt: Diagram of sites of urinary tract obstruction from kidney to urethra.
vis.caption: Sites of urinary obstruction: valves block the posterior urethra from birth. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Modern valves are caught before birth on routine scans, and four ultrasound flags raise the alarm together. The sonographer sees bilateral hydroureteronephrosis swelling both kidneys, a thick walled trabeculated bladder straining against the block, too little amniotic fluid called oligohydramnios, and the trademark keyhole sign where the dilated back urethra balloons below the bladder. That quartet is treated as valves until proven otherwise.
steps.tx: Spot PUV on **antenatal ultrasound** (pregnancy scan) through bilateral hydroureteronephrosis (both kidneys swollen), thick-walled trabeculated bladder (straining bladder wall), **oligohydramnios** (low amniotic fluid), and the **keyhole sign** (dilated posterior urethra ballooning below the bladder). Antenatal detection plans delivery near dialysis and surgery, because lung-damaging oligohydramnios plus renal dysplasia decide survival before birth.

vis.alt: Diagram of oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios causes in pregnancy.
vis.caption: Oligohydramnios in PUV: blocked urine output starves the amniotic sac. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Not all valves look alike, and the Young classification names the two that matter. Type One, causing 95 percent of cases, forms mucosal folds running down from the verumontanum to the lateral bulbar urethra like sails catching urine. Type Three is a completely different beast: a disc diaphragm with a central pinhole stretched across the channel, which the scope bursts through.
steps.tx: Classify by **Young Type I** (fold valves, **95%**, ninety five in a hundred): obstructing mucosal folds extending distally from the **verumontanum** (seminal hillock) to the lateral bulbar urethra; versus **Young Type III** (disc valves): a diaphragm with central perforation across the lumen. Type I is fulgurated along its folds while Type III is punctured through its disc, so naming the type scripts the ablation.

steps.say: A newborn in retention with failing kidneys needs draining within hours, but adult catheters would wreck the tiny urethra. Stabilization starts with a soft 5 or 6 French feeding tube threaded gently to decompress the tract, strictly avoiding large balloon catheters that split valves and false passage. Fluids and electrolytes are corrected aggressively alongside, because these babies arrive dry, acidotic, and salty.
steps.tx: Stabilise with **neonatal decompression** (urgent drainage): a **feeding tube** (soft 5F or 6F tube, five or six French) catheter decompresses the tract while large balloon catheters are banned for splitting delicate tissue. Pair drainage with aggressive fluid and electrolyte resuscitation, correcting acidosis and hyperkalaemia that accompany obstructive uropathy, before any definitive scope touches the child.

steps.say: The cure is a half hour scope, not open surgery. Transurethral endoscopic valve ablation burns or cuts the flaps at the five, seven, and twelve o clock positions using a cold knife, Bugbee electrocautery, or holmium laser through a neonatal cystoscope. Three precise nicks convert the valve into an open channel, and the bladder starts emptying before the baby leaves theatre recovery.
steps.tx: Ablate primarily with endoscopic **valve ablation** (scope destruction): incise at the **5, 7, and 12 o'clock positions** (three sparing cuts) with **cold knife** (steel blade), **Bugbee electrocautery** (button burner), or Holmium laser. The clock-face pattern divides every fold while sparing the sphincter at six o clock, so continence survives cure and most babies void freely within days.

steps.say: Sometimes nature has provided its own safety valve on one side. In VURD syndrome the blocked bladder blows out one ureter into massive reflux with a dysplastic kidney, and that venting protects the opposite kidney from the crushing pressures. The ruined side is sacrificed while the good side grows normally, so overall renal outcome beats bilateral high pressure damage.
steps.tx: Read **VURD syndrome** (valves with unilateral reflux and dysplasia) as a **pressure pop-off** (safety vent): one refluxing dysplastic unit absorbs the pressure, shielding the contralateral kidney from intravesical hypertension. Manage by protecting the good kidney fiercely while the bad side involutes, because a sacrificed moiety with a healthy mate outlives two equally battered kidneys.

steps.say: Removing the valves does not always fix the bladder, because years of pushing against resistance remodels its muscle permanently. Valve bladder syndrome leaves poor compliance with detrusor overactivity that later burns into myogenic failure, so upper tract dilatation persists despite an open channel. These bladders need lifelong urodynamic watching, timed voiding, and often overnight drainage.
steps.tx: Follow every valve child for **valve bladder syndrome** (chronic bladder damage): poor compliance (stiff storage), detrusor overactivity (unstable squeezes), and eventual **myogenic failure** (worn out muscle) sustain upper tract dilatation after ablation. Lifelong surveillance with urodynamics, anticholinergics, and clean intermittent catheterization protects kidneys through adolescence, because the bladder, not the valve, becomes the lifelong enemy.

steps.say: One blood number in the first year is used to forecast the kidneys for life. A nadir creatinine below zero point eight milligrams per decilitre, or seventy micromoles per litre, reached within the first twelve months predicts durable renal function through childhood. Babies who never dip below that line march toward dialysis, so the first year diaries of fluids, infections, and drainage decide decades.
steps.tx: Trust the **nadir serum creatinine** (lowest kidney number) under **0.8 mg/dL** (zero point eight, **70 micromol/L**, seventy micromoles) within the first year as the top **prognostic indicator** (future telling number) of lasting renal function. Sub-0.8 nadiers grow into working kidneys while higher floors herald chronic disease, so chase the nadir with perfect drainage and infection control from week one.
